newsitem.title: UK: BIB offers interactive services to BSkyB's BDB.
newsitem.headline: BIB offers interactive services to BSkyB's BDB.

text.p: British Interactive Broadcasting, the company led by BSkyB and British Telecommunications, said on Monday it was in formal talks about offering its interactive television services to British Digital Broadcasting (BDB).

BDB, also 33 percent owned by BSkyB, is a group of TV giants bidding for rights to offer digital terrestrial television (DTT) in Britain. An alliance with the similarly-named BIB had been expected since initial talks were announced earlier this month.

"BIB is determined to make the benefits of interactivity available to as many digital television viewers as possible, via compatible satellite, terrestrial or other means of distribution," said BT's director of multimedia services Rupert Gavin.
The deal will allow digital terrestrial TV customers to bank, shop, book holidays and access ticketing information and public services over their TV sets.
BIB, which also includes Midland Bank and Matsushita, aims to subsidise sales of set-top boxes, or decoders, which viewers need to receive the signals, so that many consumers will buy them.
BIB is already subsidising decoders for BSkyB's digital satellite service -- a 200-channel digital service, which is expected to be launched next year.

Digital terrestrial TV will be launched in mid-1998. Viewers of both digital satellite and digital terrestrial and viewers will need a decoder. However, one should be compatible for both services at an extra fee.
Digital satellite set-top boxes are expected to retail at around 200 stg each. No retail price for digital terrestrial decoders has yet been mooted.

It hopes to make money by taking a cut from shopping and banking transactions carried out partly over BT's network, charging a fee for use of bandwidth space, and additional revenue from advertising or sponsorship.

Two groups have bid for three key digital terrestrial TV licences to be awarded by the Independent Television Commission. The licences will allow the groups to offer at least 15 pay channels and a number of online services.

BDB, which also includes TV companies Carlton Communications and Granada Group, plans to offer a 12-channel basic subscription package, including three from the BBC BBC.CN, plus three premium channels showing sports and movies.
Its rival is Digital Television Network (DTN), wholly owned by cable and transmission company NTL Inc.

DTN plans 23 TV channels, aiming to combine local services and educational programming alongside the usual pay TV mix of sports and films. It also plans an ambitious range of home shopping and banking services.
The ITC is expected to announce its decision on the DTT licence applications by the end of June.
